item.title: Making rivals depend on your system is the secret to America's 300-year winning streak
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British, and the Americans took turns as top dog—not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake everything on their maritime system. Once they can't live without your sea lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the deadliest weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British, and the Americans took turns as top dog—not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake everything on their maritime system. Once they can't live without your sea lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the deadliest weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks down America's 300-year winning streak into a five-step strategy, then pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinions.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’is not madness but a modern power strategy. Mead says post-Cold War US diplomacy relied on 'letting the whole world know where America's red lines are' as a pillar of stability, while Trump profits from the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in other people's minds; as long as you keep moving forward, the dogs bark but the caravan passes. Trump scaled that insight to industrial proportions. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since WWII accelerate their unraveling.

10:00 The final step of global hegemony is cutting off
The Anglo-American maritime order won not through a single battle but a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital flowed in; then global trade, Dutch merchant ships plying the world, wealth so abundant that paintings showed Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada globally. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of imitating Spain's colonial blockades, invite everyone in to do business; the British navy fought pirates, and all merchant ships benefited; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. The final step is the trump card: once the other side can't live without your grain, rubber, and sea lanes, cut them off—Germany in WWI suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber cut off, and its economy collapsed.

16:38 All of China's efforts are about preventing the umbilical cord from being cut
Viewing China through the same framework, you see Beijing knows its own vulnerability. Mead says, suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan; the US could counter-blockade from 100 miles off Taiwan's coast: oil can't get in, manufactured goods can't get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina become void—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this concern is always present. So China's energy policy must be read in parallel: on one hand, building oil reserves on a scale that surprises outsiders; on the other, ramping up solar and hydro while mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia; it's the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of 'dependence on the outside world.' He also warns America not to retreat into isolationism—agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

25:50 Every technological dividend needs new institutions to match
Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, the land was full of independent farmers; building a bridge might be nice, but it raises my taxes—that trade-off itself is political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, as the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, growing a national market; in the 20th century, the suburban single-family home replaced the family farm, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth distribution machine. Today that machine hits housing prices: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. Commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, and usable housing land grows with the square of the radius; the physical space technology opens could support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional 'infrastructure'—he coins the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate for centuries has been four rhetorics: Hamiltonian wants a strong state to pave the way for capital; Wilsonian wants to spread liberal democracy; Jeffersonian fears big government; Jacksonian is isolationist in peacetime but hits back hard when attacked. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamiltonian and Wilsonian, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the tent. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies liked to say 'we're a global company, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us'; AI competition turned tech into a matter of national destiny. Economic positions shifted too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets; Silicon Valley wants supply chain and IP security, even wants employees to be patriotic, thinking selling code to China is shameful—colleagues will report you. The commercial core shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The more equipment a great power has, the more it fears technological generational shifts
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later, progress was unimaginable. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually with only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is 'how to evacuate the wounded'—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, accompanied by a swarm of drones hunting the enemy's attack drones. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front line. The change flips every six months. The irony for America: the great power with the most tanks and carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this parameter revolution—existing equipment goes from advantage to sunk cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet is trapped at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The most important new variable in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success to cross the threshold—if it fails, it's catastrophic for the initiator. But between 'attack' and 'do nothing' lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change the facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not the US attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly said that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned quickly when facing a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations factor in Japan, will be the key to the Taiwan issue in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds when the opponent is 100% convinced that 'if I do X, you will inevitably do Y, and you can and will do it.' As long as there's a human veto point in the decision chain—'I might soften at the last moment'—the commitment has a crack. Automating part of diplomatic decisions and handing them to AI turns retaliation into an executable, hesitation-free mechanism—deterrence becomes more credible. But that's the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilization-ending scale no longer require humans to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the issue is 'very interesting and somewhat puzzling,' and he doesn't think an answer has emerged yet.

item.title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Gave Back Searches and Paddlings

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, thereby narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, thereby narrowing the boundaries of those rights.

Each case is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key rulings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools in one go.

5:10 Flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse
Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and idolatry, so they refused to salute or pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and parents could be fined or jailed. In 1943, the Supreme Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinions; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 Official prayer struck down as unconstitutional
During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding "Under God" to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, interdenominational prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. Districts that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale ruled 6–1 that it was unconstitutional—not because it was mandatory, but because the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: "It is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties"; the same power that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

18:31 Armbands are constitutional expression
In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to class to protest US involvement in Vietnam. School officials announced in advance that those who refused to remove them would be suspended, yet some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 for the students. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption of schoolwork, school officials could not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared: "It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." This "substantial disruption" test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

24:40 School-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teenage pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled 5–3 for the school. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": the paper was funded by the school, readers would assume school endorsement, and the two pieces were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not cruel and unusual
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in the US. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with a stated maximum of one to five swats; but Ingram received more than 20 swats in a single incident and required medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by "the harsh fact of criminal conviction and incarceration." Schools are open institutions, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states, actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students, and disabled students paddled at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Backpack search needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the bathroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued digging and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the search was legal. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required for police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

item.title: Criticism That Lands: Give High Standards and Trust First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/

item.description: Criticism is more likely to be accepted not by leading with praise, but by showing the other person: the standard is high, and you have potential. item.content:encoded:
Criticism is more likely to be accepted not by leading with praise, but by showing the other person: the standard is high, and you have potential. In the experiment, a single sentence — "the standards are high but you can meet them" — drove Black students' revision rates to the highest.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism and translates the intervention into a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of dense information, no generic communication platitudes.

1:04 Identity bias makes people choke in the moment
When a situation carries a negative stereotype about one of your identities, and the situation matters to you, you worry about being judged according to that label. That worry comes from the situation itself; it immediately depresses performance on tests, sports, or intellectual tasks, and over time makes people avoid such situations, which in turn affects who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety comes not from ability but from the expectation of being defined by a label.

3:10 Social media corners people with labels
Social media's power lies in rapidly spreading caricatures of group images; people have no patience for nuance or exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations where one feels "I'll be seen through my identity." It occasionally spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone is negative, and the result is that in a diverse society, everyone becomes more vigilant about their identity and what others might think.

6:16 A 15-minute self-reflection can raise grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students constantly worry about the possibility of being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they value most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the opportunity to signal to the teacher "I'm more than that label," and their grades began to rise, entering a positive feedback loop: higher grades → less vigilance about the label → higher grades. The intervention is extremely low-cost yet changes long-term trajectories.

9:20 In diverse settings, the vigilance dilemma: remember or forget
The author calls this state "churn." In situations where people from different identity backgrounds interact and the stakes are high, individuals oscillate between two choices: remembering "others may interpret me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or forgetting that and relaxing to trust the people in front of them. This is not fragility but real situational pressure; when the stakes are high, it continuously drains attention that should go to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In an experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Two delivery methods — direct feedback or a "positive halo" first — were trusted by White students but highly distrusted by Black students. A third method added just one sentence: "We have high standards because the essay will be published; I've read your essay and believe you can meet them." Under this condition, the proportion of Black students who took the essay home to revise was three times that of the other conditions.

14:26 Never assume others already trust you
Having served as dean and provost for many years, Claude believes the most useful ability is recognizing that every person you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, but in reality, others worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders excel at giving this signal first: even if employees disagree with a decision, if they feel respected as individuals and for their potential, the team atmosphere changes completely.

17:35 Let people see you as human before talking trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what the situation means to them; when power is unequal, the higher-status person must release safety signals first. Second, near-paranoid clarity — beating around the bush destroys valuable information. Third, warmth and goodwill — people need to confirm the other person is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt summarizes it as connection, clarity, and care.

item.title: Latin Won't Train Surgeons: Make Exams Hard, Not Just Difficult
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin won't train surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'harder means sharper minds,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty exams.
item.content:encoded:
Latin won't train surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'harder means sharper minds,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty exams.

Placing imperial civil service exams, military selection, and modern transfer experiments on the same chain of evidence, this episode rarely bridges history and talent assessment, and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms even smart candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing imperial exams at least four times. After his final failure, on the road home he had visions, believed he was Christ's younger brother, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion—which Daisy calls possibly the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around 30 million. Failed candidates weren't just Hong: exam slots were far fewer than applicants, many kept trying into their forties and fifties, and the only way back home was teaching. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they mastered the eight-legged essay but knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young minds can only practice rigid formats, the nation bleeds in two directions at once.

22:51 British civil service reform was elite self-replication
The Northcote-Trevelyan Report is often seen by Britons as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy supports the revisionist view: under the banner of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Balliol's master, Benjamin Jowett, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students across the empire. Michael Coolican's 'No Tradesmen and No Women' argues that the 1854 report reduced the most blatant buying and selling of offices but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been developing. Exams can select people, but what they test determines whether they select for merit or for people like oneself.

35:58 Bureaucracies without price signals correct via corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to lack of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so departments don't know if their plans save or harm. The military seems a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err in peacetime too; Britain's first year of nearly every war after long peace bred crises, like the shell crisis of WWI. What forces change isn't internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a more brutal correction mechanism than prices. To make bureaucracies reliable, first create a signal that reveals consequences; otherwise, no matter how rigorous the exam, it can't save the quality of daily decisions.

43:06 Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy reminds us that in Victorian times Britain's true pillar was the Royal Navy, not the army. As early as 1677, after successive defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys introduced an oral exam for lieutenants: three senior officers grilled candidates on how to command a ship. For over a century thereafter, navigation, charting, and trigonometry entered written exams; Nelson, Cook, Flinders, and Bligh all passed through this gate as chart-makers. Daisy highlights two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One served navigational safety, the other served class distinction—naturally different outcomes.

47:31 Content irrelevant? Macaulay's screening theory misses a key link
Here's the episode's highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. In essence, whatever a generation teaches, the top performers will be the smartest, most diligent, and most honor-seeking youths; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its best students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek, and the best Cherokee speakers would still be outstanding; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it as the most practical speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy bluntly says it's more like being carried away by his own eloquence, completely missing that 'what you learn really matters.'

51:21 Dead branches and corn: wrong content makes discipline wasted water
Daisy uses Abraham Flexner's 1917 rebuttal to close Macaulay. Flexner said proponents of mental discipline are like Egyptian priests: they plant a row of dead branches and water them on schedule for discipline. If you plant corn, you get the same discipline plus a harvest. In contrast, American medical schools forced aspiring doctors to study Greek and Latin before touching medicine; Flexner's answer: medicine itself is hard enough, and using it to train the mind is far more efficient than ancient languages. Daisy agrees: spending the best years of the most talented on disproven or useless knowledge only benefits rivals who teach their youth real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: people practiced estimating rectangle areas until they improved markedly, then estimated triangle areas—transfer was almost nil. If even such similar tasks don't transfer, the claim that classical languages sharpen the brain is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer occurs only when new and old tasks share components; far transfer is largely broken. Daisy derives a design principle: to select navigators, test navigation and trigonometry; to select doctors, test medicine. Effective exams connect difficulty directly to real tasks.

item.title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Poured into AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/

item.description: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

This episode ties US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets into one capital chain, offering a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a cure-all.

0:33 Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
Don't take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the roughly 50-50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism, meaning the participants were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the fundamental issue: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive the AI investment, the sooner the punishment
Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any internet giant that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the most FOMO quarter across the entire supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, as inventory is depleted and price increases take effect, the negative factors will appear together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced leasing-to-own to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing leasing-to-own. In its latest report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—possibly partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from leasing-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial maneuvers to sustain market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

33:21 Primary market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
The answer lies in fund raising timing. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large language models, and two major chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the state's playbook. So this is not a rational long-term increment but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 New property policy removes households from the financing chain
The key of recent property policy is not to rescue developers but to detach households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing objects in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the home later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers purchase completed homes and only act as consumers, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, aiming to stabilize the denominator of the asset side first, avoiding panic during chain dismantling amid declines. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

1:01:34 Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
A slow bull isn't achieved by shouting; it's achieved by layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, functioning close to a price stabilization role; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short—not allowing short-term household money to be invested in ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises grow bigger with each rescue; at least one and a half bubbles
Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have increasingly relied on printing money to intervene in crises, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so another larger wave of easing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have at least one and a half bubbles accumulated. Central bankers have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis appears, with the endogenous result of inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensifying simultaneously. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face some form of prolonged stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
